problems.title: Overhead per element
problems.statement: Loop body: 2 useful instructions; overhead: 3 (increment, compare, branch).
hints: Overhead is paid once per unrolled iteration.

problems.title: Separate accumulators
problems.statement: One warp sums 1,024 values (already in registers) with FADD latency 4, one issue per cycle.
hints: Each add waits for the previous on the same accumulator.
problems.solution: (a) About 4,096. (b) About 1,024 plus a short combine: ~4×. The result differs in the last bits, which is why the compiler won't do it for you.

problems.title: Reassociation
problems.statement: Which transformations does the compiler perform for floats under default settings?

options: Contract a·b + c into an FMA
Split a sum into 4 partial sums
Unroll a loop with a constant trip count

problems.solution: FMA contraction is on by default in nvcc (it changes rounding, but is allowed), unrolling and hoisting are exact. Splitting sums and reciprocal division need fast-math.

problems.title: Interchange for coalescing
problems.statement: for j: for i: a[i][j] += 1 on a row-major array, where threads are assigned to the inner loop's index across a warp.

parts.prompt: Sectors per warp access as written (rows 4 KB apart)?
After interchanging so threads take j?

hints: Contiguous index should be the thread index.
problems.solution: 32 versus 4: interchange (or the equivalent thread mapping) puts the contiguous index on the lanes. It's legal here because iterations are independent.

problems.title: Loop-invariant code motion
problems.statement: A loop of 1,000 iterations computes base = ptr + row * pitch inside the body, though row and pitch never change.

parts.prompt: Instructions saved by hoisting (2 per computation)?

problems.solution: 1,998 instructions. Compilers do this routinely when they can prove nothing in the loop changes the inputs, which aliasing can prevent.

problems.title: Fusing four elementwise kernels
problems.statement: Four kernels in a chain, each reading one FP32 array and writing one, n elements.
problems.solution: 32 versus 8 bytes: 4×. Chains of elementwise ops are the bread and butter of ML compilers' fusion passes.

problems.title: When fusion needs a halo
problems.statement: Kernel 1 produces y; kernel 2 computes z[i] = y[i−1] + y[i] + y[i+1].

parts.prompt: Can a fused kernel compute z with each thread producing only its own y[i]?
options: No: z needs neighbours' y, so blocks must also compute (or exchange) a halo of y

problems.solution: A stencil consumer needs producer values from neighbouring threads, so the fused kernel recomputes the halo at block edges or shares it through shared memory. Legal, but no longer free.

problems.title: Legality of interchange
problems.statement: for i: for j: a[i][j] = a[i−1][j+1] + 1. The dependence distance vector is (1, −1).

parts.prompt: Is interchanging the loops (j outer, i inner) legal?
options: No: the distance becomes (−1, 1), lexicographically negative, so a value would be read before it's written

hints: Interchange permutes the distance vector's components.
problems.solution: Legal transformations keep every distance vector lexicographically positive. (1, −1) becomes (−1, 1): illegal. Skewing first (j' = j + i) makes it (1, 0) and then interchange is fine: the polyhedral model automates exactly this reasoning.

problems.title: Remainders
problems.solution: 125 and 3. The remainder needs a cleanup loop or predication; when n is a compile-time multiple of 8 the compiler drops it.

problems.title: Strength reduction
problems.statement: A loop of 1,000 iterations computes the address base + 4·(i·stride) each time.
problems.solution: 2,000 multiplies become one precomputed increment plus an add per iteration. This is how 64-bit address arithmetic disappears from good SASS.
